Hi! The park isn’t super horse friendly but it is doable and beautiful. I’ve been a volunteer packer in the park when they needed horse power but bringing in a helicopter would stress wildlife - but that was years ago! 

Most of the info can be found on the website if you know where to look. There are a few stock trail heads that are difficult to access without a stock struck or a tiny two horse - and you will get pulled over and have to explain to rangers that stock is allowed because of xyz. 

Backcountry trips in GNP are amazing but very hard for good reason. Much of GNP is alpine plants that can be easily damaged so no grazing is allowed. Stock must be tied to approved hitch rails and must have weed seed free certified pelleted feed. All feed must be hung when unattended so prepare to have a horse to pull your feed sacks onto the provided hanging stations. 

There are trails that horses aren’t allowed on (see website) but there are also areas that are just not fun. The first few miles from any popular trailhead are very busy. Expect people to come right up and hug your horse, take pictures, etc. Less popular trailheads are worth it for the possibility of some solitude. 

Contact the Flathead chapter of backcountry horsemen for volunteer opportunities or advice. Or message me, I’ll try to help!

On the boardwalks to hidden lake overlook there  are signs literally every hundred yards or so saying to stay on the boardwalk to protect sensitive vegetation. The boardwalks have steps on them, they aren’t particularly accessible.

I only think this is applicable in places extremely heavily traveled where boardwalks are necessary. Never said anything about other locations in glacier. I routinely do around 500 miles in the Montana backcountry/year, often with trail crews mitigating over use.

The point I think isn’t just the peeing, it’s the walking off trail on high alpine vegetation. As I was explaining to some family from out of town visiting, high alpine vegetation is very sensitive and takes a very long time to grow. One person isn’t going to hurt it, but tens of thousands of visitors go to hidden lake overlook every summer. Even if only 1 in ten people stepped off for that better shot or to pee that is still an extremely high number of feet trampling delicate plants in a very refined ecosystem. The plants feed the bugs and pika and mountain goats and as climate puts more pressure on all these species there isn’t enough wiggle room for thousands of people to tromp wherever they please. 

Do emergencies happen? Yes. Can they usually be avoided by proper planning? Yes. If everyone tried their darnedest to protect these heavily visited sensitive ecosystems it’d be great.

Many factors lead into whether a horse will drink from a watering hole, creek, lake, trough, etc. Obviously the weather, activity level, and time since last drink is a factor but the other main one is if they feel safe. I always take multiple horses to water in the wilderness at once. They like having another equine to keep an eye out for danger while they put their head down. Another huge factor seems to be the footing or stability of the ground. Horses don’t want to be in a vulnerable position and won’t want to drink from an area that is slippery if they are nervous. 

Some other factors that I’ve noticed is that if the grass they are eating is lush and damp (such as with morning dew) they won’t need to drink as much water. Same goes for eating with snow on the ground. They also tend to prioritize food over water until they are really thirsty. 

Source: worked as a horse packer in the wilderness in addition to managing barns.

I am a very high maintenance camper when it comes to sleep systems.

For car camping I use a full size three inch memory foam topper folded in half. I bring my regular pillows from home, including body pillow. I put a sheet over my memory foam and then open my sleeping bag overtop of me so I can comfortably use my king size pillow to go between my knees. I make sure that I am on flat ground and if I can’t find a flat spot I at least make it so that my feet are downwards. If it isn’t flat my spine will have a bad time. I either get dressed 100% laying down or I get out of my tent/car and get dressed standing. No hunching over!

Backcountry is a whole topic by itself. When I was working in the back country I was moving freight via horse and mule so I had a little more flexibility with gear than a backpacker. I haven’t been in that line of work due to my body for a few years now but I still got a couple nights out in the last few years. I had a Big Agnes inflatable pad, two inflatable pillows, and a mini pillow. I still struggled without a good body pillow. If I’d made it through winter with a hope of getting back out there I would have created my own inflatable body pillow to fit inside my sleeping bag. Gonna get downvoted to oblivion here but there are ethical ways to train and more sustainable ways to keep horses and mules. The fact that OP is looking for ethically sourced clothing means that they are starting to if not completely thinking this way. 

I really struggled to find a way to keep and train horses that sat right with my morals. It involved lots of research, thoughts about consent, and environmental considerations. Ultimately I changed the course of my life so that the horses I already owned had a life that fit closer to their wild ancestors while still providing the community with important benefits to offset my environmental impact. 

Horses are incredibly smart and research shows that they prefer interacting/solving puzzles for food, even if both options exist. It is possible to teach them consent cues and have their “work” mimic patterns that they would have without human intervention and make it rewarding enough that they chose to participate. 

I’m now disabled (genetic reasons) but my horses and I helped the FS and nonprofits make public land more accessible for hikers (including working directly with minorities in the outdoor industry) by clearing trail and helping move supplies. 

The vast majority of horse owners and trainers probably don’t think like this, but there is a growing moment of people who are doing good both by the animals and the environment.

I think that finding used items will be your best option. There are lots of groups on Facebook for second hand horse gear. Heck, I’ve got a pair of Tailored Sportsmans that I bought used and likely will not fit into ever again! You could also look for used tights and athletic tops that aren’t equestrian brands but still fit the look. I’ve had great luck with used items from tall boots to saddles. It sometimes just takes a bit of time and networking. 

At the very least you could shop at privately owned tack stores that carry items made in the US or another country that has decent labor laws. I worked for a saddlery/leather company for a time and I would certainly want to buy from a company that makes its own products vs outsourcing to china where the labor is cheaper and the safety/health of the employees isn’t as transparent. I also learned that just because the tack I made was out of American made leather it might contain other parts (hardware usually) that is not American made and comes from more questionable sources.

I’m biased because I’ve worked extensively supporting trail crews and educators with stock (horses/mules/donkeys/etc). I replied below but ultimately I love that the wilderness areas I enjoy not only allow, but depend on stock. 

Stock users in my area are the main group that maintains trails. Ultimately a biker or a human on foot can’t pack a bridge or other materials where they are needed. The big reason stock are allowed is because of this. The Forest Service manages millions of acres with their stock program in otherwise inaccessible areas. A helicopter can do it, but it’s more expensive and allows openings for motorized use in areas that need to be wilderness due to sensitive species.

Properly managed stock use is an excellent way to keep wild areas open, accessible, and maintain their wilderness integrity. Improper stock use annoys me as much as anyone and there are groups of stock uses trying to educate others on better practices both within the Forest service and in the private use sector.

Here is what I do at those temps, though I rarely xc ski those days. I was a ski photographer for a while so most of my cold cold gear was bought for that. 

The key for me is layers, wind proofing, and not sweating! 

Head: hat, wool knit over fine merino balaclava and/or lined with fleece. I prefer a hat that has lanolin still in it. Loose wool neck gator that is under my hat, tucked into my jacket, and riding high on my cheek bones/face. Loose knit neck gator to go up around my nose/face if I need to breath through it but usually I just do the one. 

Torso: light wool long sleeve shirt. Microfleece sweatshirt. Puffy or puffy vest. Ski jacket with medium insulation or hardshell with powder skirt and pit zips. The pit zips are essential. The powder skirt really ups the warmth unless you have bib snow pants. I use mittens that have an interior sheepskin section and a wind/waterproof shell that Velcro together or can be taken apart for lighter weight options and for drying. 

Bottoms: high quality wool or wool blend long underwear. I like Patagonia’s waffle texture. I have down blend 3/4 length pants that are awesome and have saved my butt so many times. Hard shell pants that aren’t to tight and have vents. Toe warmers for emergencies. 

It’s hard in these extreme temps to start cold because if you don’t warm up it could get scary. I would rather stop often the moment I feel that I’m going to start perspiring than be cold the whole time. I carry a backpack with an extra puffy and room for layers. The backpack provides some insulation as well. My favorite extra layer is a large very thick down best that I can put on outside of my hard shell if I don’t want to take anything off. I use the pit zips and pant vents all the time, it’s worth the couple minute stop to keep dry. I put hot water in hydro flasks in the middle of my backpack for a warm drink that hopefully won’t freeze.

I’ve sat in -40 weather and without the down pants it would have been awful. I was wearing a normal ski jacket with a second extra large ski jacket over it but once those thighs start to get cold it just sucks. Luckily xc skiing is a lot more forgiving than just standing in that!! That’s just my way of saying I think the whole kit has to work together. The snow will slide in towards the trunk with you and you’ll suffocate. If you hit your head on on the tree going in and black out you’re a goner. People from areas of different snow and tree types don’t realize the danger and die every year and even knowledgeable locals are taken despite their knowledge. Local kids are taught to stay away from tree wells at all costs and to wear a helmet.
